citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot in the oriented $3$-sphere, let $N(K)$ be a chosen closed tubular solid-torus neighborhood, let $E_K=\overline{S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}N(K)}$, and let $T_K=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$. Let $\mu$ be the positive oriented meridian, meaning the boundary of a positive normal disk in $N(K)$, and let $\lambda$ be a preferred longitude, meaning a degree-one parallel of the core $K$ in $N(K)$ that is null-homologous in $E_K$. Assume that $[\mu],[\lambda]$ are an ordered basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$, with the boundary-orientation convention $\mu\cdot\lambda=-1$. A slope is the unoriented isotopy class of an essential simple closed curve on $T_K$ whose homology class is $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$ for coprime integers $p,q$ not both zero; $(p,q)$ and $(-p,-q)$ represent the same slope. For a slope represented by $p[\mu]+q[\lambda]$, the Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is obtained by gluing an oriented solid torus $D^2\times S^1$ to $E_K$ by an orientation-reversing boundary homeomorphism that sends $[\partial D^2\times\{1\}]$ to that slope; the filled orientation agrees with the fixed orientation on $E_K$. If $q\ne0$, the coefficient is written $p/q$; the meridional slope is $1/0$, and integer $n$-framed filling means slope $n[\mu]+[\lambda]$. The oriented homeomorphism type is independent of the gluing map once its meridian image is fixed.

Assume countable choice as in the chosen tubular-neighbourhood data. Let $K$ be a smooth oriented knot with chosen exterior $E_K$ and boundary torus $T_K=\partial E_K$, and let $p:T_K\to K$ be the projection of the chosen normal-disk tube. Orient each normal disk so that its positive tangent direction followed by its oriented normal basis agrees with the orientation of $S^3$. A **meridian** $\mu$ is the oriented boundary of one such normal disk. A **degree-one parallel curve** is a simple closed curve $\lambda$ in $T_K$ for which $p|_\lambda:\lambda\to K$ has degree $+1$. A **preferred longitude** is a degree-one parallel curve satisfying $i_*[\lambda]=0$ in $H_1(E_K;\mathbb Z)$, where $i:T_K\hookrightarrow E_K$ is inclusion. This is a condition on a curve; this definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Reversing the orientation of $K$ reverses the orientations of both $\mu$ and any degree-one parallel curve. If a subgroup $P\le\pi_1(E_K,x)$ is specified using a path from $x$ to $T_K$, record it only up to replacing it by $gPg^{-1}$ for $g\in\pi_1(E_K,x)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial smooth knot and let $p,q$ be coprime integers, not both zero. The Dehn filling $E_K(p/q)$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$ if and only if $q=0$, in which case $p=\pm1$ and the slope is the meridional slope $1/0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth knot that is not ambient isotopic to the standard unknot, let $E_K$ be its chosen compact exterior, and let $T_K=\partial E_K$. There is no properly embedded disk $D\subset E_K$ whose boundary is a simple closed curve in $T_K$ that is not null-homotopic in $T_K$.

Let $V=D^2\times S^1$ and $V'=D^2\times S^1$ be solid tori, with meridian curves $\mu=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$ and $\mu'=\partial D^2\times\{1\}$. Suppose $h:\partial V\to\partial V'$ is a homeomorphism and there is an isotopy $H_t:\partial V'\to\partial V'$ through homeomorphisms, with $H_0=\mathrm{id}$, such that $H_1(h(\mu))=\mu'$. Then $h$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline h:V\to V'$. The extension may be chosen to carry the product core $\{0\}\times S^1$ onto the product core of $V'$, and has the same orientation sign as $h$ with respect to the boundary orientations.

Work in the smooth category ([[def-smooth-manifold]]). Fix once and for all the
three-sphere as the one-point compactification

$$S^3:=\mathbb R^3\cup\{\infty\}$$

of Euclidean three-space, carrying its standard smooth structure, and fix the
standard orientation of $S^3$: the orientation induced by the standard
orientation of $\mathbb R^3$ under the one-point compactification, so that the
charts of the standard atlas away from $\infty$ are orientation-preserving and
the orientation is that of a connected oriented $3$-manifold in the sense of
[[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. For $r>0$ write
$\overline B_r:=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lVert x\rVert_2\le r\}$, the closed ball of
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]] with the following restriction convention. Smoothness on a closed ball means
local extension to a smooth map on an open neighborhood in Euclidean space;
smoothness on $M\times I$, for a smooth manifold $M$ without boundary, means
local extension across $t=0,1$ in $M\times\mathbb R$. Thus these closed domains
are not asserted to be manifolds without boundary in the cited definition.

**Links.** The **standard oriented circle** is the circle
$S^1=\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with its standard counterclockwise orientation,
regarded as a smooth $1$-manifold; a
**finite disjoint union of oriented circles** is a smooth manifold
$C=S^1\sqcup\dots\sqcup S^1$ ($k$ summands, $k\in\mathbb N$)
diffeomorphic to the disjoint union of $k$ standard oriented circles. An
**oriented link** (with $k$ components) is a smooth embedding

$$L\colon C\longrightarrow S^3$$

of such a disjoint union in the sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. So $L$ is
injective, is an immersion, and is a homeomorphism onto its image with the
subspace topology, and its image $L(C)$ is a finite disjoint union of smoothly
embedded circles. Thus every link considered here is finite and tame: the
smoothness of $L$ is exactly the standing convention, and no polygonal or other
tame model is used. The **components** of $L$ are the images of the individual
summands, and the number of components is $k$.

**Ambient isotopy.** Let $I=[0,1]$. An **ambient isotopy** of $S^3$ is a smooth
map

$$H\colon S^3\times I\longrightarrow S^3$$

such that $H_0=\mathrm{id}_{S^3}$, each $H_t\colon S^3\to S^3$,
$H_t(x):=H(x,t)$, is a diffeomorphism ([[def-diffeomorphism-and-local-diffeomorphism-of-manifolds]]),
and each $H_t$ is orientation-preserving with respect to the fixed orientation.
The last clause is in fact automatic: $t\mapsto H_t$ is continuous in the
$C^\infty$ topology of the diffeomorphism group, the orientation sign is locally
constant in $t$, and $H_0=\mathrm{id}$ is orientation-preserving, so it is kept
only for emphasis.

**Equivalence of links.** Two oriented links $L_0\colon C_0\to S^3$ and
$L_1\colon C_1\to S^3$ are **equivalent** (written $L_0\sim L_1$), or
**ambient isotopic**, when there are an ambient isotopy $H$ and an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:C_0\to C_1$ with
$H_1\circ L_0=L_1\circ f$. Thus parametrizations and component labels are
irrelevant, while the induced orientation of each image component is preserved. The relation is an equivalence relation on links:
it is reflexive with $H=\mathrm{id}$, transitive by composing isotopies, and
symmetric because a smooth family of diffeomorphisms has a smooth family of
inverses. An equivalence class is an **(oriented) link type**.

**Moving off $\infty$.** Because the definition of equivalence allows the
isotopy to move a link through $\infty$, the standard practice of this page is
to first apply an ambient isotopy that carries a given link into the open ball,
and only then to project; every projection and every Reidemeister move below is
read after moving the link off $\infty$ into $\mathbb R^3$ in this way. The
orientation-preserving clause in the definition of ambient isotopy is exactly
what the oriented Reidemeister moves and the oriented closure construction must
respect. The unoriented theory uses the same ambient isotopies but forgets
the orientations of the link components.

**Links in the three-sphere versus links in $\mathbb R^3$.** A link contained in
$\mathbb R^3\subset S^3$ is a link in $S^3$; conversely every link may be
assumed after isotopy to lie in $\mathbb R^3$, by choosing a point outside the compact one-dimensional image and moving that
point to $\infty$ by a smooth rotation of the standard sphere. When comparing
links already in $\mathbb R^3$, an isotopy can also be arranged to avoid
$\infty$ throughout; the track-avoidance argument is given in
[[thm-oriented-reidemeister-equivalence-theorem]].

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot, let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle, and let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. Choose a radius $\epsilon>0$ whose closed disk subbundle $D_\epsilon\nu(K)$ is contained in $\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

u(S)$ be its normal bundle ([[def-normal-and-conormal-bundles-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]), and let $\Phi_1,\Phi_2:\Omega	o N$ be two tubular neighbourhood embeddings of the same open disc bundle $\Omega=D(
u(S))$ whose restrictions to the zero section are the inclusion of $S$ ([[def-tubular-neighbourhood-of-an-embedded-submanifold]]). Assume that $d\Phi_1$ and $d\Phi_2$ induce the same isomorphism from each vertical fibre $
u(S)_p$ to the ambient normal quotient $T_pN/T_pS$. (The usual normalization makes both induced maps the identity; merely fixing the zero section is insufficient.) Then, after shrinking $\Omega$ around the zero section, the two embeddings are isotopic through tubular neighbourhood embeddings fixing $S$ pointwise. Consequently, for every compact $A\subseteq S$ there is an ambient isotopy $H_t$ of $N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, compact support, $H_t\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$ (in particular $H_1\circ\Phi_1=\Phi_2$ there), and $H_t$ fixing a neighbourhood of $A$ in $S$ pointwise; when $S$ is compact one may take $A=S$ and obtain the agreement on a neighbourhood of all of $S$, with support in any prescribed neighbourhood of $\Phi_1(\Omega)\cup\Phi_2(\Omega)$.

Let $M$ be a compact connected orientable smooth three-manifold, let $F$ be a compact connected smooth subsurface of $\partial M$, and let $N\lhd\pi_1(F)$ be normal. If a continuous disk map into $M$ has its boundary in $\operatorname{Int}F$ with class outside $N$, there is a smoothly properly embedded disk in $M$ whose boundary lies in $\operatorname{Int}F$ and has class outside $N$. No pointwise preservation of the original boundary loop is asserted.

Consequently a compact neatly properly embedded two-sided smooth surface $S$ in such a compact orientable smooth three-manifold is incompressible if and only if its inclusion induces an injection on fundamental groups, component by component. Here incompressibility means absence of a smooth embedded compressing disk, with the conventions of the indicated definition.

Use the ambient isotopy in the definition of unknotted to transport its chosen tube to a tube around the standard core $U$. Identify the transported and standard tube domains with the same normal bundle $
u(U)$. For each tubular embedding $\Phi_j$, its differential along the zero section induces an invertible smooth bundle map $L_j:
u(U)	o
u(U)$ on the normal quotient: invertibility follows because $\Phi_j$ is an embedding and is the identity on the zero section. Precompose $\Phi_j$ with the fibrewise map $L_j^{-1}$. After restricting to a common neighbourhood of the zero section, both induced normal maps are the identity; compactness of $U$ lets us choose one such neighbourhood for the whole core. Thus the hypotheses of [F5] hold. Under [A1], [L1] supplies its countable-choice premise, so an ambient isotopy identifies the tubes after shrinking. The standard disk transfers to the smaller chosen exterior. By [F6], the region between the smaller and original tube is a product boundary collar; trim or extend the disk across the product annulus so its boundary lies on the chosen exterior torus. The resulting proper disk still has essential boundary. Pull that disk across $h$ or $h^{-1}$ into the other exterior. Its parametrization is a continuous disk map with boundary in the target torus; the boundary class remains nontrivial because the boundary restriction is a homeomorphism. If the other knot were nontrivial, apply [F9] to its compact connected orientable smooth exterior, the whole smooth boundary torus as the boundary subsurface, and the trivial normal subgroup. The disk boundary lies in the relative interior of that torus, so [F9] gives a new smoothly properly embedded disk with essential boundary. This contradicts [F2]. No smoothing of the homeomorphic image disk and no replacement of $h$ by a diffeomorphism is required. Thus either both are unknotted or both are nontrivial.

Suppose both knots are nontrivial and let $\gamma$ be the slope represented by $h(\mu_K)$. Let $W,W'$ be the source and target filling solid tori with product coordinates. If $h$ preserves orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,w)$; if $h$ reverses orientation, set $g(z,w)=(z,\overline w)$. In either case $g$ has the same orientation sign as $h$ and sends the source meridian to the target meridian. If $\phi:\partial W\to\partial E_K$ is the source gluing map, define the target gluing map by $\phi'=h\circ\phi\circ g^{-1}$. It is orientation-reversing because $\phi$ is and $g,h$ have the same sign; its meridian image is $h(\mu_K)$, so it defines the filling along $\gamma$. The maps $h$ and $g$ glue to a homeomorphism of the filled manifolds. The source filling is $S^3$, hence the target filling along $\gamma$ is homeomorphic to $S^3$. By [F1], $\gamma$ is the target meridian slope; [F7] then gives the boundary isotopy in the Statement.

If both are unknotted, [F8] gives ambient equivalences from each knot to the standard unknot; composing them gives an ambient equivalence between the knots. This conclusion is independent of whether the given $h$ preserves the knot-meridian slope.

Apply [F3] to the actual boundary restriction of $h$ and the two tubular solid tori. The extensions agree with $h$ on the common boundary and therefore glue to a homeomorphism of pairs $(S^3,K)\to(S^3,K')$. By [F3] the ambient orientation sign is the same as that of $h$. Together with steps 1.1, 1.2, and 2.1 this proves every case.
